item.title: Water and Care — Wed Sep 2, 9:00 AM — Online
item.description:
This online Working Papers Seminar, organized by Riikka Prattes, brings together Geneviève Minville and Marta Gentilucci to explore the intersections of water, care, ecology, and extraction. Their papers examine coastal communities affected by environmental change and sand extraction in the Philippines, and the politics of knowledge, technology, and deep-sea mining in the Arctic. Respondents are Brunella Casalini and Rossella Alba.

item.title: DMI/MEMS Signature Lecture Presented by Prof. Chiara Daraio — Wed Sep 2, 12:00 PM — Fitzpatrick Center Schiciano Auditorium Side A
item.description: Abstract: Architected materials typically derive their mechanical properties from continuous, rigidly connected networks of struts, plates, or shells. In this talk, I will introduce an alternative design paradigm based on discrete, topologically interlocked building blocks: polycatenated architected materials (PAMs). Inspired by chain mail, PAMs consist of rings, polygons, or polyhedral cages concatenated into three-dimensional networks derived from crystalline lattice topologies, with kinematic degrees of freedom set by particle geometry and catenation pattern. I will first describe our earlier work on two-dimensional interlocked fabrics, showing how jamming can be triggered by external confinement to reversibly and dramatically stiffen chain mail sheets, and how a modified Maxwell criterion predicts the in-plane and out-of-plane rigidity of torus-knot tessellated fabrics from their connectivity alone. item.title: Welcome Back to Campus: Reception for “Against Nature" — Thu Sep 10, 5:00 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description: The Ackland welcomes back faculty, students, and staff to campus with a celebration for its newest installation in the ART& space, Phaan Howng: Against Nature. In Against Nature, artist Phaan Howng positions an ornate botanical composition above wainscotting that suggests the architecture of a late nineteenth-century study or parlor. The paneling’s mint green tint evokes the green interior paints used in that period, achieved through harmful additions of arsenic. Above the wainscotting, painted vinyl banners depict a jungle of barely contained foliage with spikes and fronds of neon reds, electric oranges, cerulean blues, and bruised purples. During the evening, we will be celebrating with non-alcoholic drinks and snacks. Phaan will be present during the evening to mingle with attendees. item.title: Ackland Film Forum: "Z" (Costa-Gavras, 1969) — Mon Sep 14, 7:30 PM — The Lumina Theater
item.description:
Yves Montand, Jean-Louis Trintignant, and Irène Papas headline this electrifying political thriller. A politician is assassinated in broad daylight, setting in motion an investigation that gradually exposes the distance between official narratives and lived reality. Racing ahead with remarkable urgency, Z channels late-1960s anti-authoritarian currents and the growing sense that democratic institutions can no longer be taken at face value. This film will be introduced by Professor Henry Veggian, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. It will be screened at 7:30 p.m. at The Lumina Theater (620 Market St, Chapel Hill, NC 27516). Tickets are free for all audience members, and registration is required via The Lumina’s webpage. When this link is live, click to reserve your free ticket. UNC-Chapel Hill students can receive CLE credit for attending by scanning the QR code at the event.

item.title: “She Will Be Quite a Manager”: From Plantation Owner to Girl Boss — Thu Sep 17, 5:30 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description: What do a Civil War-era plantation owner and a modern “girl boss” have in common? More than you think. Adelicia Acklen and Dorothy Thomas were two of the most powerful plantation-owning women—one in the US South and the other in South America—but both wielded the power of ownership by deploying and playing on particular ideas of femininity. This talk hosted by Carolina Public Humanities traces their unsettling legacy into the present, asking what happens when women gain power within systems built on inequality. Free, but space is limited; registration is required via the Carolina Public Humanities event webpage. About the speaker: Tanya Shields is an Associate Professor of Women’s and Gender Studies whose research focuses on Caribbean studies and plantation logics. She teaches courses on the Caribbean, the arts of activism, growing up girls globally, and the continuing influence of plantation economics and politics. She is currently working on her second monograph, Gendered Labor:

item.title: Luminary & Freedom Stories — Fri Sep 18, 7:00 PM — Bennett Place State Historic Site
item.description:
During this special luminary program, Bennett Place invites you to reflect on the end of the Civil War as a momentous step towards freedom for all Americans and the end of chattel slavery in the United States.
Walk among 3,310 luminaries - one for every 1,000 enslaved people in North Carolina - and reflect on experiences of enslavement and freedom. Historians dot the path and share stories of people's pathways to freedom and life after slavery & the Civil War.
---
Harriet Ann Daves recalled just how monumental Civil War surrenders were for her family: "When the surrender came my grandfather came to my mother and told her: 'Well, you are as free as I am.'"
Claiming freedom was not so straightforward for the 331,059 enslaved women, children, and men in North Carolina during the Civil War. item.title: Ackland Film Forum: "Dog Day Afternoon" (Sidney Lumet, 1975) — Mon Sep 28, 7:30 PM — The Lumina Theater
item.description:
Al Pacino and John Cazale lead one of the defining crime films of the 1970s. What begins as a poorly planned Brooklyn bank robbery soon becomes a public spectacle shaped by television cameras, police theatrics, and an increasingly invested crowd. Made in the aftermath of Watergate, the film finds humor, empathy, and absurdity amid a pervasive atmosphere of social distrust. This film will be introduced by Professor Rick Warner, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature, Director of Film Studies. item.description:
Jada Pinkett Smith, Queen Latifah, and Vivica A. Fox anchor this energetic reworking of the heist film. After a series of setbacks leaves four Black women with few viable paths forward, they embark on a string of increasingly audacious bank robberies. Blending humor, suspense, and tragedy, Set It Off captures both the bonds of friendship and the pressures of race, gender, and economic inequality in 1990s urban America. This film will be introduced by Professor Daelena Tinnin-Gadson, UNC-Chapel Hill Department of English and Comparative Literature. item.title: Mixed-Media Floral Greeting Cards — Fri Oct 30, 10:00 AM — Duke Gardens–Pelham-Cullen Classroom in the Barnes Welcome Center
item.description: In this guided mixed-media workshop with Patricia Efunsade, founder and creative director of SaKredJoi Art, participants will create a series of botanically inspired greeting cards using a simple and approachable collage process. Begin by creating an 8.5 x 11-inch collage master sheet—a mixed-media process rooted in experimentation, layering, composition and storytelling through paper. Participants will then transform the paper into four unique handmade cards with designs that feature hand-cut flowers, stems and leaves. Everyone will complete four finished greeting cards, with the option to add personal words or sentiments. This workshop is designed to be both relaxing and creatively engaging, with a clear process that allows participants of all experience levels to leave with finished work that is ready to send or frame. All materials provided. Fee: $45; 20% discount for Duke Gardens members with discount code. Parking: Parking fees apply. Location: Pelham-Cullen Classroom inside

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Sat Nov 28, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Sep 1 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence — Tue Sep 1, 10:00 AM — Kings Mountain Historical Museum
item.description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.
The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Tue Sep 1, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources
